claims.text: The as-deposited protective coating has a uniform microstructure.
The as-deposited coating contains coexisting FCC and BCC phases.
The as-deposited coating lacks a controlled precipitate gradient.
A tailored thermal-mechanical process can induce a lamellar or gradient microstructure in the coating.
The processing sequence can create a controlled distribution of nanoscale precipitates at FCC/BCC phase boundaries.
Nanoscale precipitates at FCC/BCC interfaces act as barriers or pinning centers for dislocations.
Interfacial nanoscale precipitates reduce dislocation mobility.
Reduced dislocation mobility delays the accumulation of plastic deformation under continuous loading.
Delaying plastic-deformation accumulation improves the coating's creep resistance.
Under identical loading conditions, the engineered coating will have a lower creep rate than the uniform-microstructure control.
Under identical loading conditions, the engineered coating will take longer to develop plastic instabilities than the uniform-microstructure control.
The uniform-microstructure baseline develops progressive plastic deformation during continuous loading.
The proposed creep-resistance improvement operates under sustained stresses close to the coating's yield strength.
The proposed improvement operates only over temperatures that preserve alloy phase stability.
